title: TypeScript error patterns versus C# exceptions
hook: C# enforces typed exceptions at compile time — you can only throw Exception-derived types and catch specific ones. TypeScript runs on JavaScript where anything can be thrown, so the language uses unknown, Result unions, and runtime instanceof instead of CLR-style typed catch.

blocks.text: In **C#**, `throw` requires a **System.Exception**-derived object. `catch (IOException ex)` is a **compile-time filter** — other exception types bubble past. The **Common Language Runtime (CLR)** walks the stack, runs **finally** blocks, and preserves **StackTrace** with `throw;` (not `throw ex;`). In **TypeScript**, there is no CLR — exceptions are ordinary JavaScript throws. The catch variable is **unknown**. You cannot write `catch (e: HttpError)` and expect the runtime to filter; you narrow inside the block. For expected failures, both ecosystems increasingly prefer **Result** / **TryParse** over hot-path exceptions — but C# still throws from the Base Class Library (BCL) while TypeScript libraries mix throw, reject, and callback errors.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET runtime that unwinds the stack on throw. JavaScript engines do similar stack walks but with untyped thrown values.
entries.example: C# throw new IOException() — CLR finds catch (IOException ex).

entries.plainDefinition: Core .NET APIs that predominantly throw exceptions. Node and browser APIs mix styles.
entries.example: int.Parse throws FormatException; TS Number('x') returns NaN.

entries.plainDefinition: C# pattern returning bool with out parameter for expected parse failure — analog to Result<T, E>.
C# catch clause condition — catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == 429). No TypeScript equivalent on catch.
entries.example: Retry only throttling without catching all HTTP errors.

blocks.text: Engineers moving between C# backends and TypeScript frontends or Node services hit a culture clash: C# teaches typed catch and Try-methods; TypeScript teaches unknown, Result, and middleware mapping. Misapplying C# habits — annotating catch as Error without instanceof — causes production crashes. Misapplying TS habits — returning Result from every C# repository method — fights the BCL. Knowing which language gives compile-time catch filters versus runtime narrowing is a common staff-level interview topic.

blocks.title: Same goal, different tools
blocks.body: Both ecosystems want: expected failures as data (Result/TryParse), exceptional failures as throw, normalization at boundaries, and no empty catch in workers. The syntax differs; the architecture rhymes.

items.title: Bad user input
items.body: C#: return false from TryParse or Result. TS: Result<{ ok: false, error }> — not throw per field.

items.title: Transient I/O
items.body: C#: catch TimeoutException / when 429, retry. TS: catch unknown, instanceof or code check, retry.

items.title: Programmer bug
items.body: C#: let NullReferenceException bubble. TS: let throw bubble or use assert never in dev.

items.title: Wrap at boundary
items.body: C#: new OuterException(msg, inner). TS: new HttpError(502, msg, { cause: inner }).

diagram.title: C# CLR vs TypeScript JS error flow
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph CSharp[C#]
    T1[throw Exception only] --> U1[CLR unwind]
    U1 --> C1[catch IOException typed]
    C1 --> F1[finally / using]
  end
  subgraph TypeScript[TypeScript]
    T2[throw anything] --> U2[engine unwind]
    U2 --> C2[catch unknown]
    C2 --> N2[instanceof / Result]
    N2 --> F2[finally same keyword]
  end

snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: TryParse for expected parse failure — no exception. Lines 10–13: when filter catches only 429 — compile-time catch type plus runtime filter. Line 17: throw; preserves StackTrace.

blocks.title: TypeScript versus C# error model
rows: throw; preserves — throw ex; does not

blocks.title: Pretending TypeScript has C# catch filters
blocks.body: catch (e: HttpError) does not stop other throws from entering — there is no runtime filter. All throws enter catch; you narrow with instanceof inside.

blocks.title: Throwing strings in TS because JS allows it
blocks.body: C# developers sometimes throw strings in TS out of habit from old JS tutorials. Always throw Error (or subclass) so stack and cause work.

blocks.text: Staff interviews probe whether you architect boundaries, not memorize keywords. C# ASP.NET Core middleware catches and maps exceptions to ProblemDetails; Express uses error middleware with instanceof — same layer, different runtime. C# records and TS discriminated unions both model errors as data. Performance: exceptions are expensive on hot paths in both runtimes — Result for CSV rows is idiomatic in either language. Distributed systems: neither instanceof nor catch (RpcException) survives JSON — use stable error codes on the wire. Async: C# Task exceptions must be observed; TS Promise rejections need .catch or unhandledRejection handlers. Strong candidates articulate when to mirror TryParse in TS and when to let fetch throw once at the controller edge.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Result union — no throw in loop

snippet.label: Anti-pattern — fake typed catch
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–7: annotating catch parameter as HttpError is a TypeScript lie — no CLR filter. Lines 11–19: unknown + instanceof is the correct TS equivalent of C# catch (HttpError ex).

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming TS catch (e: HttpError) filters like C#. Saying C# can throw strings. Not knowing throw; vs throw ex; in C# when discussing TS rethrow. Ignoring that both prefer Result on hot expected-failure paths.

interviewTakeaways: C# throw is typed; TypeScript catch is unknown — narrowing replaces compile-time catch filters.
TryParse / Result struct in C# maps to Result<T, E> unions in TypeScript for expected failures.
cause in TS parallels InnerException; throw; in C# parallels rethrowing the same Error in TS.
60s: C# typed catch and when filters. TS unknown plus instanceof. Both use Result on hot paths. Wire error codes not class names. No fake typed catch in TS.
Follow-up: how do unobserved Task exceptions compare to unhandled Promise rejections?
commonPitfalls: catch (e: HttpError) without instanceof — annotation does not filter runtime throws.
Assuming C# and TS handle async errors identically — observe Task vs catch Promise rejections.
Strong answer: 'CLR typed catch vs TS unknown narrow. TryParse maps to Result. cause maps to InnerException. Stable codes on the wire.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript error patterns exist because JavaScript throw is untyped. C# never had this problem at compile time.
